title: American Radio Relay League, Inc. v. FCC (2008)
shortTitle: American Radio Relay League, Inc. v. FCC (2008)
summary: An agency that relies on its own staff studies in a rulemaking must disclose them in full for comment, and it must give a reasoned explanation for a technical choice that commenters challenged with empirical data.
notes:
Key line: "It is quite another thing to provide notice and an opportunity for comment on only those parts of the studies that the Commission likes best." (Rogers, J.)

Citation: 524 F.3d 227 (D.C. Cir. 2008).

sections.Parties: The petitioner was the American Radio Relay League, Inc., the national association of licensed amateur radio operators. The respondents were the Federal Communications Commission and the United States. Intervenors supporting the Commission included Ambient Corporation and other companies and utility groups interested in delivering broadband internet service over electric power lines, known as Access Broadband over Power Line or Access BPL. The League had sought the Commission's field studies under the Freedom of Information Act before petitioning for review, and it challenged two Commission orders adopting and then clarifying rules for Access BPL systems under Part 15 of the Commission's rules.
sections.Material Facts: Access BPL devices installed on power lines transmit radio frequency energy across the 1.7 to 80 MHz spectrum and can interfere with licensed services on the same frequencies. After a notice of inquiry in April 2003 and a proposed rule in February 2004, the Commission adopted a rule on October 28, 2004, imposing emission limits and interference remedies. It kept the existing extrapolation factor of 40 decibels per decade for frequencies below 30 MHz to estimate how emissions decay with distance. The Commission said its conclusion that the interference risk was low rested in part on its own field tests, but it denied the League's FOIA request for those studies and, in December 2004, after the rule issued, placed five staff studies in the record with parts of pages redacted as deliberative. On reconsideration in August 2006 it dismissed three 2005 British studies supporting a 20 decibel factor in one sentence.
sections.Procedural History: The League petitioned the Commission for reconsideration of the October 2004 order. The Commission denied reconsideration with a clarification on August 7, 2006, 21 F.C.C.R. 9308. The League then petitioned the United States Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit for review of both orders under 47 U.S.C. section 402 and 28 U.S.C. section 2342. The case was argued on October 23, 2007, before Judges Rogers, Tatel and Kavanaugh. The Commission offered the unredacted pages to the court, which reviewed them in camera. On April 25, 2008, the court granted the petition in part and remanded the rule to the Commission without vacating it.
sections.Issue: The League raised four claims. Whether the Commission silently abandoned its longstanding interpretation of section 301 of the Communications Act that unlicensed devices must cease operation when they cause harmful interference. Whether the Commission violated the notice and comment requirements of 5 U.S.C. section 553 by relying on staff field studies that it never disclosed in unredacted form for comment. Whether retaining the 40 decibel per decade extrapolation factor was arbitrary and capricious given the absence of empirical support and the Commission's refusal to engage with the British data. And whether the Commission adequately considered a proposal to confine Access BPL to the 30 to 50 MHz band.
sections.Holding: The court rejected the first and fourth claims. The Commission had applied its existing definition of harmful interference to a new technology after finding that residual interference to mobile amateur operations after a 20 decibel notch would not be harmful, and it had given a reasoned explanation for rejecting the band restriction. The court granted the petition on the second and third claims. Redacting portions of studies on which the Commission relied violated the APA's notice and comment requirement, and the League had shown prejudice because the redacted pages appeared to contain information in tension with the Commission's conclusion. The conclusory dismissal of the 2005 studies was not a reasoned explanation for retaining the extrapolation factor. On remand the Commission had to make the unredacted studies available for comment and either justify the 40 decibel factor or adopt another.
sections.Reasoning: Judge Rogers relied on the circuit's Portland Cement line of cases, which construes section 553 to require an agency to make available the technical studies and data it employs so that interested persons can point out errors or improper inferences; it is not consonant with rulemaking to promulgate rules on data known only to the agency. The Commission had chosen to rely on the five staff studies and to place them in the record, so it could not cherry pick the parts it liked and hide parts that might contain contrary evidence, inconvenient qualifications, or explanations of methodology. EchoStar was different because the undisclosed staff analysis there merely cogitated on evidence already in the record, and the FOIA deliberative process privilege could not cloak scientific studies the Commission had adopted in its dealings with the public. The holding was narrow: the court imposed no new procedure but enforced the Commission's own procedural choice, which distinguished Vermont Yankee. On the extrapolation factor, the Commission had itself acknowledged that the factor was important in determining compliance, that it could be determined empirically, and that the 1989 regulation applied only pending development of an appropriate measurement procedure. The NTIA study it cited cast doubt on the factor, the modeling results it relied on were not in the record, and its one sentence dismissal of the British studies offered no discernable path for the court to follow under State Farm.

topics.lrs-o-rulemaking-record: The panel enforced study disclosure under circuit precedent; Kavanaugh’s separate opinion disputed its basis without overruling it.
topics.lrs-n-hard-look: The court also remanded for the FCC's failure to give a reasoned explanation of its extrapolation factor, an arbitrary-and-capricious holding separate from the disclosure issue.

learning.separateOpinions: Judge Tatel concurred, emphasizing that the whole record requirement of APA section 706 independently requires disclosure of the complete studies, because selective redaction of evidence that fairly detracts from the agency's conclusion would defeat meaningful arbitrary and capricious review, citing Walter O. Boswell Memorial Hospital v. Heckler and Kent County v. EPA. Judge Kavanaugh concurred in part, concurred in the judgment in part, and dissented in part. He accepted the disclosure remand as required by binding Portland Cement precedent but argued that the doctrine cannot be squared with the text of section 553 or with Vermont Yankee, and he dissented from the extrapolation factor remand, finding the Commission's short explanation sufficient under State Farm and warning that judicially expanded procedures had made rulemaking a laborious, never ending process.
